nameStory: The Club Foot gets its memorable name from its distinctive bulbous stem base that swells out like a wooden club or baseball bat handle. When you spot this mushroom in the woods, that swollen 'foot' at the bottom of the stem is usually the first thing that catches your eye and makes identification easy.
description: Club Foot is a medium-sized gilled mushroom with a grey-brown cap and a telltale swollen stem base that looks like it's wearing oversized boots. The cap typically ranges from 2-4 inches across and starts convex before flattening out with age. Its most distinctive feature is the bulbous stem that tapers from a thick, club-like base up to a thinner top. The yellowish gills run down the stem (called 'decurrent'), giving it a characteristic funnel-like appearance.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Distinctively club-shaped with a swollen, bulbous base that tapers upward - feels firm and solid when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Grey-brown color, smooth to touch, starts dome-shaped but flattens with age, often with slightly wavy edges

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Yellowish to cream-colored, running down the stem (decurrent), creating a funnel effect toward the center

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, mild mushroomy odor - not unpleasant or strongly distinctive

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White to cream-colored when spores are collected on paper overnight

habitat: Look for Club Foot in both deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, where it grows from the soil among leaf litter and fallen branches. It's particularly common in mixed woods with oak, maple, and pine trees. This fungus prefers moist, rich woodland soil and often appears in small scattered groups rather than large clusters.

seasonality.spring: Rarely appears in late spring. Spend this season learning the forest habitats where you'll find Club Foot later in the year.
seasonality.summer: Begins fruiting in mid to late summer, especially after periods of warm rain. Look for the characteristic bulbous stems emerging from forest duff.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for Club Foot! Most abundant from August through October when forest moisture levels are ideal. The grey-brown caps blend well with autumn leaves.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting stops with cold weather. Old, dried specimens may persist but lack identifying features.

funFact: Club Foot contains a compound that creates a dangerous reaction when combined with alcohol - similar to the medication used to treat alcoholism - causing nausea, flushing, and rapid heartbeat that can last for hours even from small amounts of beer or wine consumed days after eating the mushroom!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other Clitocybe species, but the dramatically swollen stem base of Club Foot is usually distinctive enough to separate it from look-alikes. Remember: 'Club Foot has the boot' - that bulbous base is your key identifier that other similar brown, funnel-shaped mushrooms lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'potentially edible' in some guides, Club Foot should never be eaten due to its dangerous interaction with alcohol and its resemblance to truly poisonous species. The genus name was recently changed from Clitocybe to Ampulloclitocybe, so you may see it listed under either name in older field guides.
compareHints: Since Club Foot is the only Ampulloclitocybe species commonly found in New England, compare it to other funnel-shaped mushrooms in the Waxcap family. Unlike true waxcaps which have waxy, often brightly colored caps, Club Foot has a matte, grey-brown appearance. The combination of decurrent gills, grey-brown coloring, and that unmistakable club-shaped stem makes it unique among New England fungi.
